You have THREE related GitHub issues, in this exact order, as three SEPARATE PRs, each fully merged before you start the next:

## 1. Issue #1196 — PR #1219 already open, finish it first
`gh issue view 1196` for full text (caps `unexpected_index_list` at capture time in `gx_runner._extract_sample_failures` for pandas-backed datasources). Review the actual diff (`git log -p` on this branch vs main) to see exactly what was implemented. Then:
- Run the `/code-review` skill (Skill tool) against PR #1219's diff. Fix blocking findings in a follow-up commit + push. File a GitHub issue for anything genuinely deferred.
- Wait for CI green, then squash-merge (`gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`) if clean.

## 2. Issue #1197 — start after #1196 is merged
`gh issue view 1197` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`'s `_RedactionTracker.record()` OR-accumulates a column's "was it shown" state across BOTH `unexpected_index_list` and `partial_unexpected_list` when both are present. Each list is classified independently (value-based heuristic over each list's OWN sample) — so the same column can classify "shown" against one list and "masked" against the other. Since the tracker ORs toward "shown", a column masked in `unexpected_index_list` (the list the frontend actually renders, per merged PR #1190) but classified shown in `partial_unexpected_list` gets excluded from `redacted_columns` / undercounted — even though every cell for that column in the DISPLAYED list reads masked. Display-honesty bug, not a PII leak (whichever list renders has its own cells correctly masked), reopening the #424/#1115 class.
Fix: classify/track against the SAME list the frontend displays — if a dict-shaped `unexpected_index_list` is present, track only from that list; otherwise track from `partial_unexpected_list` (keep existing #1115 anonymous-mask semantics for the scalar-list path). Add a regression test with a dual-list sample where the tested column masks in the index list but shows in the partial list — assert the label reflects the DISPLAYED (index) list. Keep existing #1115 tests green.
- `git checkout main && git pull && git checkout -b fix/issue-1197-redaction-tracks-displayed-list`. Implement, test, Black/Ruff/mypy, commit (`Fixes #1197`), push, open PR, set milestone, run `/code-review`, fix blocking findings, wait for CI green, merge if clean.

## 3. Issue #1203 — start after #1197 is merged
`gh issue view 1203` for full text. Summary: `run_service.py::_build_result` does `observed = {"error": outcome.error_message}` for an errored check, passing GX's `exception_info.exception_message` through verbatim. On a SQL execution engine (Snowflake, Unity Catalog) this is typically a SQLAlchemy `StatementError` whose `str()` appends `[SQL: ...] [parameters: (...)]`, and warehouse errors commonly quote the offending CELL VALUE. This lands in `results.observed_value`, OUTSIDE the sample_failures retention sweep and OUTSIDE the suite's column-redaction policy — reaches run-detail API, UI, alerts, MCP output unredacted. Same shape #989 already fixed for monitors.
Fix: strip the `[SQL: …] [parameters: …]` tail STRUCTURALLY — SQLAlchemy exposes `.statement`/`.params` on `StatementError`, check those attributes, NOT a regex-on-prose hack — keep the driver's own first line. Do NOT apply a blanket scrub (would regress usability — see `SafeMonitorError`'s docstring for why that distinction was drawn). Regression test: construct/simulate a `StatementError` carrying a parameter value, run through `_build_result`, assert persisted `observed_value` does NOT contain that value or the `[SQL:`/`[parameters:` tail, but DOES retain the driver's first-line message. Must work identically for Snowflake and Unity Catalog (shared path, no per-datasource divergence).
- `git checkout main && git pull && git checkout -b fix/issue-1203-sql-exception-cell-leak`. ## 2. Issue #1197 — start after #1196 is merged
`gh issue view 1197` for full text. Summary: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`'s `_RedactionTracker.record()` OR-accumulates a column's "was it shown" state across BOTH `unexpected_index_list` and `partial_unexpected_list` when both are present. Each list is classified independently (value-based heuristic over each list's OWN sample) — so the same column can classify "shown" against one list and "masked" against the other. Since the tracker ORs toward "shown", a column masked in `unexpected_index_list` (the list the frontend actually renders, per merged PR #1190) but classified shown in `partial_unexpected_list` gets excluded from `redacted_columns` / undercounted — even though every cell for that column in the DISPLAYED list reads masked. Add a regression test with a dual-list sample where the tested column masks in the index list but shows in the partial list — assert the label reflects the DISPLAYED (index) list. Keep existing #1115 tests green.
- `git checkout main && git pull && git checkout -b fix/issue-1197-redaction-tracks-displayed-list`. Implement, test, Black/Ruff/mypy, commit (`Fixes #1197`), push, open PR, set milestone, run `/code-review`, fix blocking findings, wait for CI green, merge if clean.

## 3. Issue #1203 — start after #1197 is merged
`gh issue view 1203` for full text. Summary: `run_service.py::_build_result` does `observed = {"error": outcome.error_message}` for an errored check, passing GX's `exception_info.exception_message` through verbatim. On a SQL execution engine (Snowflake, Unity Catalog) this is typically a SQLAlchemy `StatementError` whose `str()` appends `[SQL: ...] [parameters: (...)]`, and warehouse errors commonly quote the offending CELL VALUE. This lands in `results.observed_value`, OUTSIDE the sample_failures retention sweep and OUTSIDE the suite's column-redaction policy — reaches run-detail API, UI, alerts, MCP output unredacted. Same shape #989 already fixed for monitors.
Fix: strip the `[SQL: …] [parameters: …]` tail STRUCTURALLY — SQLAlchemy exposes `.statement`/`.params` on `StatementError`, check those attributes, NOT a regex-on-prose hack — keep the driver's own first line. Do NOT apply a blanket scrub (would regress usability — see `SafeMonitorError`'s docstring for why that distinction was drawn). Regression test: construct/simulate a `StatementError` carrying a parameter value, run through `_build_result`, assert persisted `observed_value` does NOT contain that value or the `[SQL:`/`[parameters:` tail, but DOES retain the driver's first-line message. Must work identically for Snowflake and Unity Catalog (shared path, no per-datasource divergence).
- `git checkout main && git pull && git checkout -b fix/issue-1203-sql-exception-cell-leak`. Implement, test (including the existing tests from #1196/#1197 you should re-run to confirm nothing regressed), Black/Ruff/mypy, commit (`Fixes #1203`), push, open PR, set milestone, run `/code-review` (take findings seriously, security-adjacent), fix blocking findings, wait for CI green, merge if clean.

input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ. A prior agent session was interrupted by an account spend-limit error mid-task. Resume the work — do NOT start over, and do NOT just merge as-is.

Existing state: `cd /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-af26f477cbdfa98de` — existing git worktree, branch `fix/issue-1109-lineage-first-call-abort`, PR **#1220** already open (`gh pr view 1220`), CI all green (14/14). Read CLAUDE.md in that worktree's root first.

Background: issue #1109 (`gh issue view 1109`) is about `SnowflakeLineageProvider._from_get_lineage` in `backend/app/lineage/warehouse_snowflake.py` — an unclassified error on the FIRST `GET_LINEAGE` call used to abort the whole pull; the fix makes it descend to lower tiers instead (skip just that tier, classified reason, let the union answer), since the per-seed traversal now makes up to 2N calls and a transient blip on call 1 shouldn't cost the whole graph.

**A `/code-review` pass already ran on this PR before the session was interrupted, and found a real, substantive regression that was NOT yet fixed.** Read the PR's existing state (`git log -p` on this branch vs main, and `gh pr view 1220 --json body,comments`) to see the current diff. The key finding to address:

**The core problem:** swallowing the unclassified first-call GET_LINEAGE failure and treating it as a degraded-but-successful result means `fetch_edges` returns a normal `WarehouseLineageResult` instead of raising. That result flows through `_persist` in `backend/app/lineage/warehouse_refresh.py`, which — since `SnowflakeLineageProvider.is_incremental` is False — PRUNES the snapshot's `lineage_edges` down to just the floor/ACCESS_HISTORY tier for that cycle, on EVERY transient GET_LINEAGE blip. This directly contradicts `warehouse_refresh.py`'s own documented "#828 never-prune-on-unavailable" invariant (a transient blip should never wipe previously-cached richer edges). Additionally, `refresh_connection_lineage` clears `connection.lineage_last_error` to None and counts the connection as "refreshed" on this degraded path — understating a real recurring problem.

Secondary findings from the review (address if you can do so cleanly, otherwise file follow-up issues — don't let scope balloon and block the primary fix):
- The fix is ordinal-based (only call #1 is protected) — calls 2..2N-1 failing unclassified still silently fold into `seed_failures` with a bare structlog line and no product-visible signal, even for a majority-failure run. This is PRE-EXISTING (from #892), not introduced by this PR, but the PR touches exactly this code path — per CLAUDE.md's "don't dismiss pre-existing findings" rule, this needs at minimum a filed follow-up issue if not fixed here.
- If the floor tier ALSO fails after an unclassified first-call GET_LINEAGE failure, the original GET_LINEAGE failure detail is discarded before `fetch_edges` raises `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` — no test covers this combined-failure case.
- Minor: `f"call failed ({type(exc).__name__})"` doesn't distinguish "transient, may self-heal next cycle" from "structurally unsupported, permanent" in the UI-facing degraded_reason text.

**Your job:** decide and implement the RIGHT fix for the primary pruning-regression problem. The likely correct shape: when a tier is skipped due to an UNCLASSIFIED failure (as opposed to a classified `_FeatureUnsupportedError` like an edition gate or grant denial, which IS a legitimate "this tier will never work" signal), the result should be treated as non-authoritative for pruning purposes — i.e. `_persist` should NOT prune previously-cached tier data on a transient-unclassified-skip, only on a classified/confirmed-unsupported skip or a genuine confident-empty. You'll need to thread some signal (e.g. a flag or a distinct classification on `WarehouseLineageResult`/`skipped_tiers`) from `_from_get_lineage` through `fetch_edges` to `_persist` distinguishing "transient, don't prune" from "confirmed unsupported, prune is fine." Look at how `is_incremental`/prune logic currently works in `_persist` to find the right hook point. Also fix (or explicitly decide not to, with reasoning) the `lineage_last_error`/refresh-count understatement.

Write regression tests: (1) an unclassified first-call failure does NOT prune previously-cached GET_LINEAGE-tier edges on the next persist cycle (only degrades the read for that cycle); (2) a genuinely classified `_FeatureUnsupportedError` first-call failure (edition gate etc.) still allows normal pruning to the lower tier, since that's a legitimate permanent state; (3) the combined GET_LINEAGE+floor failure case still raises `WarehouseLineageUnavailableError` with useful diagnostic info.

Workflow:
1. `conda activate dataq` (never `conda run`).
2. Implement the fix on the existing branch. Re-run the FULL lineage test suite (not just new tests) plus `warehouse_refresh` tests to confirm nothing else broke.
3. Run Black/Ruff/mypy locally.
4. Commit as a follow-up commit on the same branch (conventional commit describing the prune-regression fix), push.
5. Re-run the `/code-review` skill on the UPDATED diff to confirm the fix actually addresses the finding and didn't introduce new issues. File GitHub issues for the secondary findings above if you didn't fix them in this PR (use the fixed-or-filed rule — don't drop them).
6. Wait for CI green. Only squash-merge (`gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`) if CI is green AND you're confident the pruning regression is genuinely fixed and tested. If you're not confident, leave it open and explain exactly what's unresolved in your final report.
7. Report: PR URL, merge status, exactly what you changed to fix the pruning regression, what you did about the secondary findings (fixed vs filed, with issue numbers), and your confidence level.

Gotchas: shell may be fish (quote glob flags, no `timeout`). Never `--no-verify`, never force-push. If branch is out of date with main when merging, merge/rebase main in first — this PR touches lineage files that shouldn't conflict with concurrent work in this session, but verify.

**1. `backend/app/datasources/base.py:73-78` — stale/incomplete comment on `CheckOutcome.metric_value`, not updated by this PR**
```python

metric_value: float | None = None
```
This asserts that for GX-expectation outcomes, `severity.extract_metric` always parses the metric "from the sample" (i.e. `sample_failures`). This PR adds a second source: for `unexpected_rows_expectation` (custom-SQL), the metric is now parsed from `observed_value`, not `sample_failures` — a distinct field with its own docstring above (line 43) and its own retention-purge treatment. The comment wasn't touched by this PR and is now inaccurate for that one expectation type. Minor (doesn't affect correctness, just documentation drift on a field this PR's new code path relies on) — worth a one-line fixup, e.g. "...whose metric is parsed from the sample (or, for custom-SQL, from `observed_value` — see `severity.py`)."

- Module docstring's new "Custom-SQL checks" bullet (branch order, "0 on success, the count on failure") matches the actual `if/elif/else` cascade in `extract_metric` and is verified by both `test_custom_sql_passes_on_sql_batch_without_reading_a_dataframe` (`observed_value == {"observed_value": 0}` on success) and the new severity unit tests.
- The "`severity.py` is pure (no DB/GX access)" invariant (asserted in both the module docstring and the ADR amendment) holds: `custom_sql.py` imports only `re`/`string`/`typing`/`core.errors.DataQError`, and `core.errors`/`core.logging` pull in FastAPI/structlog/otel/config — no DB or GX imports anywhere in the chain.

This is a substantive batch of findings on #1104's PR (#1227) — worth flagging clearly:

1. **Unguarded `session.commit()` inside the `except` block** with no nested try/except — if that bookkeeping commit itself fails, it aborts the entire nightly sweep for every remaining connection, not just the one that failed. Same risk on the success-path `else` branch's commit.
2. **Missing row-lock on `inventory_sync_failing_since`** — plain read-modify-write with no `with_for_update()`, a lost-update race under concurrent sweeps. The codebase has an *exact* precedent for this (`orchestration_service.record_poll_failure`'s `consecutive_poll_failures`) that explicitly uses row-locking for this reason — this PR didn't follow it.
3. **Reading stale/expired ORM attributes after `session.rollback()`** without re-fetching — `record_poll_failure`'s own docstring documents this exact hazard in this exact codebase and re-fetches deliberately; this PR reuses the stale instance instead, risking `ObjectDeletedError` if the connection was deleted concurrently.

These aren't nitpicks — they're real robustness gaps against documented precedent in the same codebase. Letting the #1104 agent work through them; I'll check in if it looks like it's heading toward merging without addressing the two race/failure-cascade issues.

The diff's core complexity driver is a design choice made in an earlier PR (#1186): `workspace_health.key` is a bare SHA-256-derived hash with no sibling detail column (justified by the 64-char PK cap vs 256-char Airflow DAG ids). PR #1235's read side has to work around that by reconstructing candidate tuples and hash-probing for hits, which creates a real coupling: the write side (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) derives tuples from one known `run_env` crossed against enabled bindings with a *different* env; the read side (`list_current_env_near_misses`) has to invert that — it doesn't know `run_env`, so it must enumerate all *other* `ENVS` members as candidates per binding. Both sides must agree on `_near_miss_key`'s exact field order/format forever, silently and without an error path if they ever drift (a mismatch just yields empty results, not a failure). This complexity is inherent to the opaque-hash storage decision, and a `NearMissRecord` dataclass + `NearMissRead` Pydantic model both duplicate the same 5-field shape across layers (normal, but worth noting).

Frontend: `nearMisses: TriggerEnvNearMiss[]` is threaded through `TriggersPanel → TriggersBody → TriggerRow`, doing a linear `.find()` per row inside the `renderItem` callback (recomputed every render).

1. **file:** `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:155-230` (`list_current_env_near_misses`)
   **summary:** Read side re-derives every one of `enabled_bindings × (len(ENVS)-1)` candidate tuples and hashes each to probe for a stored row, duplicating (in inverted form) the tuple-generation logic that `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` already owns.
   **failure_scenario:** If `_near_miss_key`'s field composition/order ever changes on one side without the other (or `ENVS` gains a member), lookups silently return empty — no exception, no test failure signal beyond a behavioral gap. Storing the decoded `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` as real columns in a small dedicated `trigger_env_near_miss` table (composite PK, `pipeline_or_dag_id` as unbounded `Text`, avoiding the 64-char cap that forced hashing in the first place) turns this into one `SELECT ... WHERE updated_at >= cutoff`, eliminates the hash-guess loop entirely, and removes the two-implementation coupling.

2. **file:** `backend/db/models.py:1248` (root cause) / `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:210-224` (`_near_miss_key`)
   **summary:** The underlying design constraint (opaque hash, no detail column, driven by `WorkspaceHealth.key`'s shared 64-char PK) is what forces the guess-and-check read pattern.
   **failure_scenario:** A dedicated near-miss table (or a JSONB detail column alongside the existing hash key, keeping the hash as dedupe PK but adding `payload: dict` for decode) would let the read side just deserialize instead of reconstructing. <result>Confirmed there is a global `DataQError` → HTTP-response mapping, which is exactly why the sibling endpoints (dry-run, profile) never need a router-level `try/except` at all — the service layer raises typed `DataQError` subclasses and FastAPI's handler does the rest.

## Findings

**Angle 1 — Altitude**

1. `_FLATFILE_TYPES` in `backend/app/services/run_target.py` (lines 128–131, 158–162) is dead-weight duplication, not a justified special case. Traced the actual call path: `preview_batch` → `resolve_target` → `resolve_target_shape` (`backend/app/datasources/registry.py:357`) → `_TARGET_RESOLVERS`. That registry has no entry for `adf`/`airflow` (raises `TargetShapeError("...has no run path...")`) and its `snowflake`/`unity_catalog`/`iceberg` resolvers all call `_require(target, "table", conn_type)`, which already raises `TargetShapeError` because a batch-shaped `{pattern, strategy, prefix}` dict has no `table` key. So for every connection type the guard rejects, `resolve_target` — called two lines later in the very same function — would already raise the equivalent `SuiteTargetInvalidError`. The guard only changes the error string, not the outcome. Its own comment ("duplicated ... rather than imported so this module's write-time validation path stays GX-free") is also empirically false: `run_target.py:43` already does `from backend.app.datasources.registry import resolve_target_shape` unconditionally at module load, and `registry.py` already does `from backend.app.datasources.flatfile import build_flatfile_runner` unconditionally at module load, and `flatfile.py:39` does `import great_expectations as gx` at module load — so importing `run_target` (which `suite_service`'s write path already does) has been loading GX transitively all along, pre-existing this PR. The stated GX-avoidance rationale doesn't hold, so there's no justification left for hand-duplicating the type set instead of calling `resolve_target_shape` directly and mapping its (already-correct) `TargetShapeError`/`SuiteTargetInvalidError`.

2. The three new error classes (`BatchPreviewNoDataError`, `BatchPreviewInvalidError`, `BatchPreviewFailedError`) and their try/except mapping live in the **router** (`backend/app/api/v1/suites.py:517–529, 561–589`). Every sibling no-persistence preview endpoint does the opposite: `dry_run_check` (`backend/app/api/v1/checks.py:452`) has zero try/except and is a pure pass-through to `dryrun_service.dry_run_check`, whose own module (`backend/app/services/dryrun_service.py:51,56,...`) defines `DryRunUnsupportedError`/`DryRunNoDataError`/`DryRunFailedError` and does the identical `BatchNotFoundError→422 / DataQError passthrough / Exception→502 w/ classify_failure_reason` translation internally. `profile_columns` (`suites.py:426`) is the same: `ProfileUnsupportedError` etc. live in `profile_service.py:91–113`, and the router has no try/except at all. Batch-preview inverts this: `run_target.preview_batch` leaks raw `flatfile.BatchNotFoundError`/`BatchListingTooLargeError` (both bare `ValueError`s) up to the router, which then has to know the flatfile module's exception types to translate them. This is an inconsistency in where error taxonomy is owned — a future service-layer caller of `preview_batch` (not the HTTP router) gets undifferentiated `ValueError`s instead of typed `DataQError`s the way every other service in this codebase behaves.

No CLAUDE.md-quotable violations found (angle 2) — the PR correctly keeps ADF/Airflow out of `_FLATFILE_TYPES`/the registry, touches no migration, and adds no tracked secret.

<result>## Assessment

This is a real altitude problem, not a nitpick. `workspace_health`'s own docstring frames it as a **write-only delivered-alert/dedupe flag** (`key` + `alerted_at` + `updated_at`, no payload) — a shape that's fine for "has this been sent" but was never designed to answer "what business tuple does this row represent." The PR needs exactly that second question and answers it by re-implementing the write side's candidate-generation logic on the read side and using it as an oracle against opaque hashes. The hash function itself (`_near_miss_key`) *is* shared code, so that part can't drift. But the **candidate-selection logic** — which `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` tuples are even eligible to be hashed — exists in two places (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` and `workspace_health_service.list_current_env_near_misses`), tied together only by a prose comment, not a shared function or a shared test. The new tests exercise the read side against the low-level write leaf (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`), never against the actual production write path (`_record_env_near_misses`), so a change to that derivation logic would ship green and desync silently in prod. `ENVS` is at least a shared imported constant with a DB check constraint on both sides, so the "new env added" risk is lower than it first appears — the sharper risk is any future change to the *selection* logic (scoping, extra conditions, disabled-connection handling), which has zero compiler/test coupling. The "no schema change" checkbox is a false economy: a `detail` JSONB column or a dedicated `trigger_env_near_misses` table would have made the read trivial and change-safe, at the cost of one migration this PR explicitly avoided.

<result>Enough context. I have a clear picture of both the backend hash-guessing pattern and the frontend prop-threading/`.find()` pattern.

## Summary

The diff's core complexity driver is a design choice made in an earlier PR (#1186): `workspace_health.key` is a bare SHA-256-derived hash with no sibling detail column (justified by the 64-char PK cap vs 256-char Airflow DAG ids). PR #1235's read side has to work around that by reconstructing candidate tuples and hash-probing for hits, which creates a real coupling: the write side (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) derives tuples from one known `run_env` crossed against enabled bindings with a *different* env; the read side (`list_current_env_near_misses`) has to invert that — it doesn't know `run_env`, so it must enumerate all *other* `ENVS` members as candidates per binding. Both sides must agree on `_near_miss_key`'s exact field order/format forever, silently and without an error path if they ever drift (a mismatch just yields empty results, not a failure). This complexity is inherent to the opaque-hash storage decision, and a `NearMissRecord` dataclass + `NearMissRead` Pydantic model both duplicate the same 5-field shape across layers (normal, but worth noting).

Frontend: `nearMisses: TriggerEnvNearMiss[]` is threaded through `TriggersPanel → TriggersBody → TriggerRow`, doing a linear `.find()` per row inside the `renderItem` callback (recomputed every render).

Findings:

1. **file:** `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:155-230` (`list_current_env_near_misses`)
   **summary:** Read side re-derives every one of `enabled_bindings × (len(ENVS)-1)` candidate tuples and hashes each to probe for a stored row, duplicating (in inverted form) the tuple-generation logic that `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` already owns.
   **failure_scenario:** If `_near_miss_key`'s field composition/order ever changes on one side without the other (or `ENVS` gains a member), lookups silently return empty — no exception, no test failure signal beyond a behavioral gap. Storing the decoded `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` as real columns in a small dedicated `trigger_env_near_miss` table (composite PK, `pipeline_or_dag_id` as unbounded `Text`, avoiding the 64-char cap that forced hashing in the first place) turns this into one `SELECT ... WHERE updated_at >= cutoff`, eliminates the hash-guess loop entirely, and removes the two-implementation coupling.

2. **file:** `backend/db/models.py:1248` (root cause) / `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py:210-224` (`_near_miss_key`)
   **summary:** The underlying design constraint (opaque hash, no detail column, driven by `WorkspaceHealth.key`'s shared 64-char PK) is what forces the guess-and-check read pattern.
   **failure_scenario:** A dedicated near-miss table (or a JSONB detail column alongside the existing hash key, keeping the hash as dedupe PK but adding `payload: dict` for decode) would let the read side just deserialize instead of reconstructing. Saves the `O(bindings × 3)` hash computation per request and the entire candidate-dict bookkeeping (`candidates: dict[str, tuple[...]]`, lines 196-207).

3. **file:** `frontend/src/components/suites/TriggersPanel.tsx:684-689`
   **summary:** `TriggerRow`'s near-miss match is a `.find()` over the full `nearMisses` array inside the `renderItem` callback, re-run on every render of every row.
   **failure_scenario:** Building one `Map<string, TriggerEnvNearMiss>` keyed by `` `${provider}|${pipeline_or_dag_id}|${binding_env}` `` once in `TriggersPanel` (via `useMemo`) and passing a single looked-up `nearMiss` (or the map itself) down would replace N `.find()` calls with N `Map.get()` calls and centralize the matching key logic in one place instead of inline in JSX — low-severity given the array is tiny (≤3× enabled bindings), but the pattern doesn't scale and obscures the match semantics at the call site.

4. **file:** `frontend/src/components/suites/TriggersPanel.tsx:641-676` (prop threading)
   **summary:** `nearMisses` is threaded as a raw prop through `TriggersPanel → TriggersBody → TriggerRow`, three layers deep, purely to be matched per-row at the bottom.
   **failure_scenario:** Minor — this is idiomatic React and the tree is shallow, so it's a low-priority nit rather than a real problem; flagged only because combining it with finding #3 (do the matching once at the `TriggersBody` level, pass each row its resolved `nearMiss` via a memoized map lookup rather than passing the whole array down) removes both the drilling-for-raw-data smell and the per-row linear scan in one change.

**Not flagged as issues:** the fail-open `nearMissState.status === 'ok' ? ... : []` resilience pattern, the `since_hours` recency window, and the `NearMissRecord`/`NearMissRead` dual-model split are reasonable and idiomatic for this codebase's layering conventions.</result>

- Exception ordering in `preview_batch_target` (suites.py ~572-596): `BatchNotFoundError(ValueError)` is caught before the broader `(BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError)` clause — correct, most-specific-first. `DataQError` (e.g. `SuiteTargetInvalidError`) is a separate hierarchy from `ValueError`, so there's no MRO ambiguity between the second and third `except` clauses.
- The React debounce/token logic in `BatchPreviewHint` (SuiteForm.tsx ~610-663): traced through Strict-Mode double-invoke, unmount, and rapid-field-change scenarios — the monotonic `token` + `clearTimeout` correctly prevents stale responses from clobbering newer state, and the unmount cleanup (`token.current = -1`) blocks post-unmount `setState`.

- The new top-level `from backend.app.datasources.flatfile import ...` in `suites.py` looks like it eagerly pulls in Great Expectations at API-startup, contradicting the "GX-free write path" comment — but `backend/app/services/profile_service.py` (already imported by `suites.py`) already imports `flatfile` eagerly, so this is not a new regression. **One concrete, substantiated bug:**

```json
[
  {
    "file": "/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-arijit-Coding-Python-DataQ/23338a22-3fe4-41f8-b4f7-1c7ba861cfd6/scratchpad/pr1233-wt/backend/app/api/v1/suites.py",
    "line": 579,
    "summary": "The `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError) as exc: raise BatchPreviewInvalidError(str(exc), ...)` branch puts the raw exception text straight into the client-facing error envelope (`DataQError.message` -> `error.message` in the JSON body, confirmed via core/errors.py's `_dataq_error_handler`). This new endpoint is the only place in the codebase that takes an arbitrary caught `ValueError` and echoes `str(exc)` back to an HTTP caller unredacted.",
    "failure_scenario": "Any future (or already-possible) bare `ValueError` raised deep inside the S3/ADLS listing path (e.g. an Azure `BlobServiceClient(account_url=..., credential=secret)` construction failure, or a boto3 client-construction ValueError) is caught by this clause instead of the generic `except Exception` 502 path, and its `str(exc)` — which can echo connection/config fragments the SDK includes in its error message — is returned as `error.message` in the 422 response. The frontend `BatchPreviewHint` component (SuiteForm.tsx ~651-660) then renders that message verbatim in the UI (`Typography.Text type=\"danger\">{state.message}`) to any user with 'edit' permission on the suite, since only the `batch_preview_no_data` code gets special-cased — every other 422, including this one, is shown as `errorMessage(err)` i.e. the raw backend message. No test in the PR (`test_batch_preview_listing_too_large_returns_422`) asserts on message content, so this would not be caught by CI."
  }
]
```

**Fix suggestion:** either narrow the clause to just `BatchListingTooLargeError` (whose message is already a fixed, safe string) and let a bare `ValueError` fall through to the generic `except Exception` → `classify_failure_reason` 502 path (matching `dryrun_service.py`'s convention), or replace `str(exc)` with `classify_failure_reason(exc)` if a 422 is still wanted for that class of error.</result>

## Findings — PR #1235 code-reuse review

**1. `cutoff = now - window` reimplemented, including twice in the same file it just edited**
- file: `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py`, line 187
- summary: `list_current_env_near_misses` hand-rolls `cutoff = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(hours=window_hours)`. The exact same idiom already exists 100 lines up in the same module (`evaluate_poll_staleness`, line 81: `reference < moment - timedelta(seconds=threshold)`), plus in `asset_view_service.warehouse_lineage_status` (`stale_before = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(hours=stale_after_hours)`) and `otp_service` (`cutoff = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(hours=older_than_hours)`).
- failure_scenario: No shared `cutoff_from_hours()`/`is_stale()` helper exists anywhere in `backend/app/core`, so this is now the 4th independent hand-rolling of "now minus a configured window" — one of them a few dozen lines away in the very file being edited. Nothing enforces the same UTC-aware, `now()`-injectable shape across all four; a future refactor (e.g. switching the reference clock, or a timezone bug fix) has to be applied in four places and will likely miss one. Should have been pulled into a tiny shared helper in `backend/app/core/` (or at minimum reused the poll-staleness comparison already in this file) rather than adding a 4th copy.

**2. Read-side candidate generation diverges from the write side it claims to mirror, instead of sharing it**
- file: `backend/app/services/workspace_health_service.py`, lines 197–207 vs. `backend/app/services/orchestration_service.py`, lines 279–288 (`_record_env_near_misses`)
- summary: The write path derives mismatch candidates by querying **actual** `TriggerBinding.env` rows for the pipeline where `env != connection.env` (only envs that genuinely have another binding). The new read path instead loops `for run_env in ENVS: if run_env == binding_env: continue` — a synthetic cross-product over the whole closed vocabulary, not the real binding set. The docstring claims it re-derives tuples "the same way `_record_env_near_misses` would have produced them," but the two implementations are structurally different.
- failure_scenario: If `ENVS` (`backend/app/db/models.py:101`) ever grows or a per-provider env subset is introduced, the two derivations silently drift — the read side would hash candidates the write side could never produce (harmless but wasted queries) or, if the closed vocab narrows, could actually miss real rows. A single `_candidate_mismatch_envs()` helper used by both callers would keep them provably in sync instead of relying on a comment to assert equivalence.

**3. Frontend `TriggerEnvNearMiss.run_env`/`binding_env` typed `string` instead of reusing `ConnectionEnv`**
- file: `frontend/src/api/triggerBindings.ts` lines 582–588, consumed at `frontend/src/components/suites/TriggersPanel.tsx` line 714
- summary: `run_env`/`binding_env` are declared as plain `string`, forcing `nearMiss.run_env as ConnectionEnv` / `nearMiss.binding_env as ConnectionEnv` casts in `TriggersPanel.tsx` just to call the existing `envLabel()`.
- failure_scenario: The existing `ConnectionEnv` type (`frontend/src/api/connections.ts:116`) already models this exact closed vocab and is used everywhere else `env` flows through the frontend (`TriggerBinding.env` is typed `ConnectionEnv`, two lines above in the same file). Typing the new fields as `string` throws away that type safety and needs an unchecked cast at the call site — an unrelated backend value change wouldn't be caught by the compiler the way it would be for every other `env` field.

**Not flagged (checked, no gap found):** `AssetHealthLead`-style "best-effort overlay" — `TriggersPanel` correctly reuses `useAsyncData` + `state.status === 'ok' ? data : fallback`, which is the codebase's established idiom (14+ other call sites), not a reimplementation. `ENVS` cross-product-as-reusable-utility — no prior generic "iterate the other members of a closed vocab" helper exists to reuse; the gap is item 2's divergence from the write side, not a missed pre-existing utility.</result>

<result>## Assessment

This is a real altitude problem, not a nitpick. `workspace_health`'s own docstring frames it as a **write-only delivered-alert/dedupe flag** (`key` + `alerted_at` + `updated_at`, no payload) — a shape that's fine for "has this been sent" but was never designed to answer "what business tuple does this row represent." The PR needs exactly that second question and answers it by re-implementing the write side's candidate-generation logic on the read side and using it as an oracle against opaque hashes. The hash function itself (`_near_miss_key`) *is* shared code, so that part can't drift. But the **candidate-selection logic** — which `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, run_env, binding_env)` tuples are even eligible to be hashed — exists in two places (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` and `workspace_health_service.list_current_env_near_misses`), tied together only by a prose comment, not a shared function or a shared test. The new tests exercise the read side against the low-level write leaf (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`), never against the actual production write path (`_record_env_near_misses`), so a change to that derivation logic would ship green and desync silently in prod. `ENVS` is at least a shared imported constant with a DB check constraint on both sides, so the "new env added" risk is lower than it first appears — the sharper risk is any future change to the *selection* logic (scoping, extra conditions, disabled-connection handling), which has zero compiler/test coupling. The "no schema change" checkbox is a false economy: a `detail` JSONB column or a dedicated `trigger_env_near_misses` table would have made the read trivial and change-safe, at the cost of one migration this PR explicitly avoided.

  {"file": "backend/app/services/orchestration_service.py", "line": "240-290", "summary": "Write-side derivation duplicated conceptually (not code-shared) in the read side", "failure_scenario": "An engineer edits _record_env_near_misses without realizing list_current_env_near_misses must mirror it exactly; discovered only when a user/QA notices psql-visible rows that never surface in the app."},

<result>Everything is confirmed merged and cleaned up. Here's the final report.

## Final Report

**PR #1222** — `perf(profiler): route Parquet sampling through the RangeReader seam (#882)` — **MERGED** (squash-merged, branch deleted). Closed issue #1001.
URL: https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1222

### What I did

1. Reviewed issue #1001 and the existing diff — the prior session had already routed the Parquet profiler sampler through the `RangeReader` seam and gotten CI green, but hadn't run `/code-review`.
2. Ran the backend test suite locally (232 targeted tests, then the full 2353-test suite) plus black/ruff/mypy/bandit on the touched files — all clean.
3. Ran the `code-review` skill against PR #1222 with `--comment`, which posted 2 inline findings.

### Blocking findings — both fixed in a new commit (`dd6c6484`)

1. **`RangeReader` opened with the wrong chunk size.** `_read_parquet_sample` used `RangeReader`'s default 256 KiB *seeking* window, but `iter_batches` does a *sequential/scattered* streaming read — the same pattern `csv_row_count` already handles by passing a larger chunk. I reproduced this empirically: on a 200-small-row-group fixture the default chunk caused 89-92 range requests totaling ~6.8x the object's own size — the "sampler" transferred *more* bytes than the whole-object download it was meant to replace. Fix: promoted `flatfile._STREAM_CHUNK` to public `STREAM_CHUNK` and passed it to the `RangeReader` in `_read_parquet_sample`. I benchmarked several chunk sizes across a spread of row-group layouts before picking this value — it isn't a strictly-under-100% guarantee in every layout (a single-window cache still occasionally re-fetches on a jump), but it caps amplification at roughly 1.0–1.4x versus the unbounded multiplier the default produced. Verified the regression test actually catches this via a mutation check (reverting the fix makes it fail with 19 requests vs. the `<10` bound).
2. **No automated test for the empty/header-only Parquet fallback path.** The PR description said this edge case was verified "by hand" only. Added `test_read_dataframe_parquet_sample_of_an_empty_file_returns_typed_empty_frame`.

Also added `test_read_dataframe_parquet_sample_uses_the_streaming_chunk_on_many_small_row_groups` to pin the chunk-size fix, and honestly loosened the pre-existing test's byte-bound assertion (from a tight `<0.6x` to `<1.5x` + a request-count check) to reflect the real trade-off rather than overclaiming.

No findings were deferred/filed — both were fixed directly.

### CI / merge

- Local: full backend suite green (2357 passed after merging main), black/ruff/mypy/bandit clean.
- Merged latest `main` into the branch (clean, no conflicts).
- Pushed; all 15 CI checks green (backend tests/lint/types/bandit/pip-audit, frontend tests/lint/audit/E2E, CodeQL ×3, secret scanning, GitGuardian).
- Replied to both review threads with what was fixed, resolved them via GraphQL (required — `mergeStateStatus` was `BLOCKED` on unresolved threads until then), then squash-merged with `Fixes #1001` auto-closing the issue.

### Follow-up

Per CLAUDE.md's post-merge convention, opened and merged a second small **PR #1237** (`docs: progress.md — record PR #1222 (fixes #1001) in the Snapshot`) updating the Open-issues count (30→29 Backlog, 50→48 repo-wide) and noting the fix — also fully green through CI and merged.

Both branches (`fix/issue-1001-profiler-sampler-range-read`, `docs/progress-1001-snapshot`) are deleted; issue #1001 is closed.</result>

## Final Report

**PR #1222** — `perf(profiler): route Parquet sampling through the RangeReader seam (#882)` — **MERGED** (squash-merged, branch deleted). Closed issue #1001.
URL: https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1222

### What I did

1. Reviewed issue #1001 and the existing diff — the prior session had already routed the Parquet profiler sampler through the `RangeReader` seam and gotten CI green, but hadn't run `/code-review`.
2. Ran the backend test suite locally (232 targeted tests, then the full 2353-test suite) plus black/ruff/mypy/bandit on the touched files — all clean.
3. Ran the `code-review` skill against PR #1222 with `--comment`, which posted 2 inline findings.

### Blocking findings — both fixed in a new commit (`dd6c6484`)

1. **`RangeReader` opened with the wrong chunk size.** `_read_parquet_sample` used `RangeReader`'s default 256 KiB *seeking* window, but `iter_batches` does a *sequential/scattered* streaming read — the same pattern `csv_row_count` already handles by passing a larger chunk. I reproduced this empirically: on a 200-small-row-group fixture the default chunk caused 89-92 range requests totaling ~6.8x the object's own size — the "sampler" transferred *more* bytes than the whole-object download it was meant to replace. Fix: promoted `flatfile._STREAM_CHUNK` to public `STREAM_CHUNK` and passed it to the `RangeReader` in `_read_parquet_sample`. I benchmarked several chunk sizes across a spread of row-group layouts before picking this value — it isn't a strictly-under-100% guarantee in every layout (a single-window cache still occasionally re-fetches on a jump), but it caps amplification at roughly 1.0–1.4x versus the unbounded multiplier the default produced. Verified the regression test actually catches this via a mutation check (reverting the fix makes it fail with 19 requests vs. the `<10` bound).
2. **No automated test for the empty/header-only Parquet fallback path.** The PR description said this edge case was verified "by hand" only. Added `test_read_dataframe_parquet_sample_of_an_empty_file_returns_typed_empty_frame`.

### The pruning regression — what I changed

The prior commit's descend-don't-abort made `fetch_edges` *return* where it used to *raise*, so `_persist` (which prunes for any non-incremental provider) wiped the snapshot down to the floor tier on every transient GET_LINEAGE blip — contradicting `warehouse_refresh`'s own "#828 never-prune-on-unavailable" invariant.

Threaded a new `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable` flag end to end:
- `_FeatureUnsupportedError` gained a `transient` kwarg, set at each raise site. **Confirmed** skips (edition gate, missing grant, genuinely-empty tier) stay prunable; **transient** ones (unclassified first-call failure, failed catalog read, half-finished traversal) set `prunable=False`.
- `_persist` gates the prune **and** the verbatim `columns` replace on one `authoritative_snapshot = not is_incremental and result.prunable`. Gating the prune alone would still have wiped column detail — the floor tier carries no column pairs, so a verbatim replace on a blipped cycle overwrites a real mapping with NULL.

3. **Wrong justification.** The `_RedactionTracker` docstring claimed comparison buckets "render as one table" — `ComparisonResultDetail.tsx` renders one `<Table>` per bucket. That sentence is the load-bearing reason the cross-bucket OR survives, so I corrected it to "separate tables, visible together in one view".

## Task 2 — #1203

**PR:** https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1240 — **MERGED**, issue #1203 **CLOSED**. Milestone `v1.1 Week 6`, matching the issue. `/code-review` at high effort returned **no findings**.

I read this in the installed SQLAlchemy 2.0.51 rather than from memory. That makes `"\n[SQL: "` a genuine structural delimiter between "what went wrong" and SQLAlchemy's rendering of `.statement`/`.params` — so `partition` at that marker removes the statement, every bound parameter, the `hide_parameters` variant and the trailing doc link, without inspecting the prose. Params can never appear without the marker. The driver's own first block is deliberately kept, per the issue's explicit warning that a blanket `classify_failure_reason` would regress usability the way it would have for `MonitorConfigError` (`SafeMonitorError`'s docstring).

Applied at three choke points so no datasource can diverge: `run_service._build_result` (every kind and runner funnels through it — Snowflake and UC share it), `dryrun_service` (the **same leak**, on the surface a broken custom-SQL check hits *first*, before it's ever saved — I found this while tracing and it's fixed here), and `run_service.redact_observed_value` (the read side that the run-detail API, MCP tools and alert builder all call — this corrects rows **already persisted in prod**, which matters because `observed_value` has no retention sweep). The strip is idempotent, so both sides cost nothing.

**Evidence quality.** Tests build a **real** `StatementError` rather than a hand-written string, so they track SQLAlchemy's actual rendering instead of my idea of it, and each asserts the premise (the parameter really *is* in the raw message) before asserting it's gone. I mutation-checked them: with the strip neutered to `return message`, all five new assertions fail. Full suite 3,742 passed.

Two things the reviewer examined and deliberately left, with reasoning recorded rather than dropped: the kept driver message can echo part of the user's own statement for some drivers, but a suite `view` recipient already sees that SQL via the check's `expected_value` kwargs, so it's not a new authz crossing; and an echo-only message would store `None` instead of `{"error": …}`, which is unreachable since `details[0]` is always the non-empty `"(mod.Name) …"` form.

Re-counted with `gh issue list` *after* the merge and fixed via https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1241 (merged) — 45 open repo-wide, 28 in `v1.1 Backlog`.

1. **Unguarded `session.commit()` inside the per-connection `except` block in `backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`'s `sync_asset_inventory`** (and the mirrored one in the success `else` branch) — if that bookkeeping commit itself fails (transient Postgres error, deadlock, pool exhaustion), the exception is uncaught and propagates out of the `for connection in connections` loop, aborting the ENTIRE nightly sweep for every remaining connection — violating the function's own documented "one broken connection never starves the rest" fail-soft contract. PR #1227 is merged and #1104 is closed. Summary:

## What was fixed

**Finding 1 — unguarded bookkeeping commit.** The outcome write moved into `_record_sync_outcome` (`backend/app/services/inventory_service.py`), which never raises and always leaves the session usable. Previously a transient Postgres error on that commit propagated out of the `for connection in connections` loop and aborted the whole nightly sweep — the fix for an invisible failure had itself acquired one.

**Finding 2 — missing row lock.** Rather than write a second lock implementation, the mechanism was extracted from `orchestration_service` into a new shared `backend/app/services/connection_lock.py` (`lock_connection`), imported by both. `inventory_sync_failing_since` is now read-modify-written under `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`, exactly as `record_poll_failure` guards `consecutive_poll_failures`. No behaviour change on the orchestration side (only the contended-lock log event was renamed; nothing consumed it).

**Finding 3 — stale ORM reads after rollback.** The sweep now snapshots `(id, type)` off fresh instances in one pass before any commit/rollback, re-fetches by id per iteration, and the bookkeeping re-reads under the lock. A vanished row is logged and skipped.

**Finding 4 — over-eager PERMISSION classification.** Gated on *phase*, not category: only a failure raised by the enumeration query itself (`InventorySyncEnumerationError`, which carries no message and is classified via `__cause__`) may claim a grant. A secret-store 403 or driver-handshake rejection now gets the generic reason. The second review pass also caught that a Snowflake role losing warehouse USAGE is rejected at the same point, so the message names role/warehouse privileges alongside the SELECT grant and hedges.

**Finding 5 — stale state on opt-out.** Cleared both in the sweep *and* in `connection_service.update_connection` when the toggle flips off — the sweep can't see a toggled-off-then-on-between-ticks window, and during a plain opt-out every reader saw "failing since <old date>" for up to a day.

**Second `/code-review` pass** found 5 more; 4 fixed in-PR (run-centric fallback wording that literally said "the run failed to execute… see the server logs" — the answer #1104 exists to replace; the grant-message hedge; the update-time clear; a stale `deploy/README.md` row). Docs: ADR 0040 §5 amended, `docs/progress.md`, snapshot counts verified post-merge (45 open repo-wide / 28 backlog — matches).

## Verification
- Every new regression test was **mutation-checked** against un-fixed code (9 mutations, all killed). One test was initially vacuous: a same-session bulk delete *expunges* the instance, and a detached instance answers `.type` from memory — so it needed `synchronize_session=False` to reproduce the prod shape.
- Full backend suite green: **3762 passed, 1 skipped, 97.1% coverage** (the three touched modules are at 100%). An earlier 841-failure run was a self-inflicted concurrent-test-DB collision, re-run clean on a dedicated Postgres.
- Migration tested up → down → up against real Postgres; single alembic head.
- Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean; full CI green; merged CLEAN.

## Follow-up filed
[#1242](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1242) — Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is **privilege-filtered, not access-denied**, so a role with no grants enumerates *zero rows* rather than raising, which this PR records as a healthy sync — leaving the Snowflake half of #1104 where it started. Deferred because an empty-by-design database enumerates zero rows too; distinguishing them needs a new state + UI decision, not a bug fix.

One note for you: `docs/progress.md`'s **Open PRs** row says `0` but there are currently **3** open PRs (other agents in this sweep) — it was already stale on main before my change, and I left it alone to avoid conflicting with concurrent work.

input.description: Fix #1193 exception-leak finding, then merge
input.prompt:
Repo: DataQ (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). Read CLAUDE.md in the repo root FIRST for the mandatory per-functionality workflow.

Work in the existing worktree at /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-afa1a98eee1196ff1, branch feature/issue-1193-batch-target-preview, which backs open PR #1233 (fixes #1193 — batch-target resolution preview endpoint + UI hint).

A prior `/code-review` pass found one real, worth-fixing-before-merge issue and two non-blocking nits:

**Blocking finding (fix this):** In the new `preview_batch_target` endpoint in `backend/app/api/v1/suites.py`, the clause `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError) as exc: raise BatchPreviewInvalidError(str(exc), ...)` echoes the raw exception text straight into the client-facing error envelope (`error.message` in the JSON response, which the frontend's `BatchPreviewHint` component then renders verbatim to any user with edit permission on the suite). Every other similar endpoint in this codebase (e.g. `dryrun_service.py`'s identical `materialize_path` try/except) routes unexpected exceptions through `classify_failure_reason(exc)` specifically because a runner/adapter exception can carry DSN, credential, or PII fragments (per `failure_classifier.py`'s own docstring) and must never be surfaced verbatim. `dryrun_service.py` doesn't even special-case `ValueError` — any non-`BatchNotFoundError`/non-`DataQError` exception there falls through to the safe `classify_failure_reason` 502 path.

Fix: narrow the clause to just `BatchListingTooLargeError` (whose message is a fixed, safe string — confirm this by reading its definition in `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py`) and let a bare `ValueError` fall through to the generic `except Exception` → `classify_failure_reason` 502 path, matching `dryrun_service.py`'s convention exactly. Add/verify a test proving a bare `ValueError` with a sensitive-looking message does NOT get echoed verbatim in the response.

**Non-blocking nits worth folding in if cheap (your judgment):**
1. `_FLATFILE_TYPES` in `backend/app/services/run_target.py` duplicates a rejection `resolve_target()` already performs two lines later via the registry's `_TARGET_RESOLVERS` (confirmed: every connection type this guard rejects, `resolve_target()` would already reject via `TargetShapeError`/`SuiteTargetInvalidError`). Its "keeps this module GX-free" rationale is also factually false — `run_target.py` already transitively imports GX at module load via `registry.py` → `flatfile.py`. Consider removing the duplicate guard and just calling `resolve_target()` / mapping its error directly.
2. The new error classes (`BatchPreviewNoDataError`, `BatchPreviewInvalidError`, `BatchPreviewFailedError`) and their try/except translation live in the router (`suites.py`) instead of the service layer, diverging from the sibling pattern where `DryRunNoDataError`/`ProfileUnsupportedError` etc. live in their respective service modules with a thin pass-through router. Consider moving the error taxonomy into `run_target.py` itself if it's a clean move; skip if it'd be invasive.

Workflow:
1. `conda activate dataq` for backend (never `conda run`); `pnpm` for frontend if needed.
2. `cd` into the worktree, `git fetch origin && git merge origin/main` to pick up everything merged since this branch was created — resolve conflicts carefully, don't force-push. Take main's version of `docs/progress.md` if it conflicts.
3. Fix the blocking finding (required). Fold in the two nits if genuinely cheap; otherwise leave them and explain why in your report.
4. Run Black/Ruff/mypy + backend tests, frontend lint/typecheck/tests, locally.
5. Commit the fix(es), push.
6. Run the `/code-review` skill again on the updated diff to confirm the fix is solid. Fix any new blocking findings; file an issue for anything genuinely deferred.
7. Wait for CI green (`gh pr checks 1233 --watch`), confirm CLEAN merge state, then squash-merge: `gh pr merge 1233 --squash --delete-branch`.
8. Confirm `gh issue view 1193` shows closed.

Report back: what you fixed, whether you folded in the nits, merge status, any follow-up issues filed.

Gotchas: shell may be fish (quote glob flags). Never `--no-verify`, never force-push.

Done. PR #1233 is squash-merged to `main` (`78a69427`) and #1193 is closed as completed.

## What I fixed

**Blocking finding (as briefed).** `except (BatchListingTooLargeError, ValueError)` echoed `str(exc)` into `error.message`, which `BatchPreviewHint` renders verbatim. `ValueError` is the *superclass* of both flat-file batch signals, so any driver `ValueError` — botocore/azure text carrying an endpoint, account, or SAS token — leaked to the client. Narrowed to `BatchListingTooLargeError` alone (confirmed safe: `flatfile._counted` builds a fixed sentence from the caller's own prefix plus our own limit); everything else falls through to `classify_failure_reason`'s 502, matching `dryrun_service`. Regression coverage at the service layer **and** over the full response envelope. Mutation-checked by restoring the `ValueError` clause — the test fails on the echoed credential string.

**Both nits folded in.**
1. Dropped `_FLATFILE_TYPES`. Verified the duplication claim in code: a batch spec carries no `table`/`path`, so `_snowflake_target`/`_unity_catalog_target`/`_iceberg_target` all reject it via `_require`, and orchestration providers have no `_TARGET_RESOLVERS` entry at all. The "keeps this module GX-free" rationale was indeed false — `run_target` → `registry` → `flatfile` imports GX at module load.
2. Moved the `BatchPreview*` taxonomy and its translation into `run_target`; the router is now a pass-through.

## Second review pass found three more, all fixed in-PR

- **Stale preview relabelled as current.** The hint kept the previous spec's answer through the whole 400 ms debounce, and re-showed it on the `active` false→true flip — clearing a `specific` batch key and typing a new one brought the *old* batch's path back as if it resolved the new key. Every non-idle state now carries the spec it describes.
- **Classified reason discarded.** The 502's message is deliberately generic, so `detail.reason` was the only actionable half, and the UI never read it. Now appended.
- **Stale comment** in `suiteTarget.ts` claiming no preview endpoint exists.

**One test-quality trap worth flagging:** my first two stale-hint tests passed *against the mutant*. An awaited `findByText` let the 400 ms debounce fire and set `loading` on its own, so the assertion held with or without the fix. They now use a bounded `waitFor` (150 ms) — a timer can fire late but never early, which is what makes them discriminating. Every fix here was mutation-checked.

## Deferred

**[#1243](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1243)** (filed, `bug`, `v1.1 Backlog`) — the preview's listing is unbounded (500k objects), blocking and uncancellable on a sync route that auto-fires on every typing pause with no client `AbortController`, and a user regex is now matched in the API process for the first time (ReDoS; `re` holds the GIL). Deferred because the fix is a design change, not a line edit, and the endpoint is authenticated, edit-gated and rate-limited.

## Verification

Local gate green before each push: Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean, backend **3793 passed** (97.11% coverage), frontend lint + tsc clean, **942 passed** with the coverage gate. All 13 CI checks passed; merge state was `CLEAN` before merging.

I also corrected the PR body, which documented the old (and, on the 502 security claim, false) error contract, and merged a follow-up **#1244** re-counting the `docs/progress.md` snapshot with `gh issue list`/`gh pr list` after the fact: 28 in `v1.1 Backlog` / 45 repo-wide (unchanged — #1193 closed, #1243 filed, netting out) and 2 open PRs (#1235, #1231).

Done. PR #1231 merged, #1108 closed.

## What I did per finding

**Finding 1 (required) — fixed.** `?status=` was validated on neither `/runs` nor `/pipeline_runs`, so `?status=succeded` — or the wrong-case `Succeeded`, since the column stores lower-case — returned `200 []` with a confident `X-Total-Count: 0`. Both now 422 against their closed vocabulary (`RUN_STATUSES` / `PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES`), raised **before** the header is computed so the error carries no total at all rather than a `0` describing a population never queried. `/pipeline_runs` reuses the existing `orchestration_service.validate_read_filters` (extended with `status`); `/runs` gets a matching `run_service.validate_read_filters`. Both vocabularies are also now documented in Swagger. Four regression tests, all mutation-checked — reverting the fix fails all four with `200 != 422`.

**Finding 2 (index) — filed as [#1245](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1245), not fixed.** The gap is **identical and pre-existing on all three tables** (`pipeline_runs` since #928, `incidents` since #772), so a `runs`-only index inside a header-shaped PR would be an arbitrary partial fix. `runs` also already has `ix_runs_suite_created` on `(suite_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)`, which covers the suite-filtered read — only the broad `suite_id IN (...)` case is uncovered. Index choice there wants EXPLAIN evidence at real row counts, which is squarely the W6 scale-aware work. The issue carries the full table inventory and acceptance criteria, including that "measured: the planner ignores it at our volume" is a valid outcome.

**Finding 3 (drift) — fixed.** Each `count_*`/`list_*` pair now shares one filter chain (`_run_filters`, `_pipeline_run_filters`, `_incident_filters`). Frontend header parsing became one `toListPage` helper — placed in a **new `src/api/listPage.ts` rather than `client.ts`**, because every API test replaces `client.ts` wholesale with `vi.mock`; putting it there broke 7 tests and would have meant the mocks stubbed out the arithmetic. In its own module it stays at 100% coverage under those mocks.

## Second `/code-review` pass — 5 new findings, all fixed

The sharpest one was real and load-bearing: **`/runs` got the header but `listRuns` discarded it**, so the Results *Runs* tab — the primary runs surface and the whole reason for #1108 — still rendered its capped 200-row fetch as if complete. Fixed by returning a `RunListPage` and adding the same disclosure the Pipeline tab has (`RecentRuns` takes only `.items`; it's deliberately a "most recent 8" widget). Also fixed: the pipeline note counted the *unfiltered* page while the table rendered filtered rows (so "Showing the most recent 200 of 211" could sit above a 3-row table or the empty state), its advice to "narrow the provider or date filter" could never work since both selects are client-side over the already-fetched page, a stale comment calling `total` "filter-scoped", and two deprecated antd `Alert message` props. Both new tests mutation-checked.

The 422 being an **undeclared breaking change** was a fair call — I documented it explicitly in the PR body rather than leaving it implied.

## Notes

- The merge of `origin/main` (~75 files) was conflict-free — no manual resolution needed, `docs/progress.md` included.
- A repo hygiene test (`test_no_test_hides_a_request_inside_an_assert`) caught one of my own shortcuts — `assert client.get(...).status_code == 200` — which `python -O` would have deleted entirely. Fixed.
- Filed a follow-up docs PR [#1246](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1246) (merged) for the post-merge re-count: **28 in `v1.1 Backlog` / 45 repo-wide, unchanged** — #1108 closing and #1245 filing into the same milestone net out. Counts taken live from `gh issue list`, not predicted.

A prior `/code-review` pass found several findings across multiple rounds. Use your judgment on fix-vs-file per CLAUDE.md's fixed-or-filed rule, but the FIRST one below is the most important and should be fixed, not filed:

1. **Access-control widening (fix this, it's a real new exposure):** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` is auth-only/workspace-wide unscoped — but `TriggerBinding` rows are suite-owned config that the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` endpoint (`backend/app/api/v1/trigger_bindings.py`) already suite-scopes (`svc.list_bindings(db, user_id=current_user.id, ...)`, docstring "List trigger bindings on accessible suites"). This PR's new endpoint lets ANY authenticated user enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for trigger bindings on suites they have zero access to — information `GET /trigger-bindings` would 403/omit for them. The route's docstring justifies this by analogy to `/orchestration/pipelines`, but that endpoint's data (`pipeline_runs`) is genuinely workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas `TriggerBinding` rows ARE suite-owned. Fix: scope the near-miss read to only bindings on suites the calling user can access, mirroring how `list_bindings` does it (likely via the same `accessible_suite_ids`-style filter used elsewhere in this codebase, e.g. in `run_service`/`incident_service`).

2. **Multiple-concurrent-near-misses-per-binding gap (fix if reasonably contained):** The frontend badge (`TriggerRow` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) picks the FIRST matching near-miss via `.find()` when more than one could be simultaneously current for the same binding (e.g. two different orchestrator connections both reporting the same DAG id against different wrong envs — literally the #1186 root cause this whole feature exists to catch). This silently hides the second live mismatch. Also related: no `ORDER BY` on the `WorkspaceHealth` read query before the Python-side sort in `list_current_env_near_misses`, so result ordering isn't guaranteed on ties, compounding the above non-deterministically.

3. **Stale badge after disabling a binding:** disabling a binding (`onChanged` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) only reloads the bindings list, never `nearMissState` — so a mismatch badge can persist on a binding the user just disabled, until the panel remounts. Fix if cheap (e.g. also trigger a near-miss refetch on `onChanged`).

4. **Test-coverage gap (fix by strengthening tests, don't need new prod code):** the new tests exercise the write LEAF (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`) directly, not the actual production write path (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) — so a future change to that function's candidate-selection logic could ship green and silently desync read vs. write with no test catching it. Add at least one test that exercises the real production write path end-to-end (trigger `_record_env_near_misses` itself, not the leaf) and asserts the read side picks it up correctly.

5. **Lower priority, your judgment (fix if cheap, else file or skip):** the hash-guessing read pattern (`list_current_env_near_misses` re-derives candidate tuples and hash-probes, rather than storing/reading decodable data) is architecturally coupled to `orchestration_service`'s write-side derivation logic by a prose comment only, not shared code — a real but not urgent debt given `WorkspaceHealth.key` is an opaque hash by design (64-char PK cap). Also: the near-miss fetch on `TriggersPanel` mount refetches workspace-wide data on every suite switch (no caching), and runs even for suites with zero trigger bindings. These are efficiency/architecture observations, not correctness bugs — fix only if trivial, otherwise file as a follow-up issue rather than silently dropping.

## Summary

**PR #1235 merged** (squash, `9a9dc957`), **#1199 closed**, branch deleted. Merged main first (clean, no conflicts).

### Findings addressed

**1. Access-control widening (fixed — this was the real one).** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` shipped auth-only by analogy to `/orchestration/pipelines`. The analogy was wrong: `pipeline_runs` is workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas a near-miss is derived *wholly* from `trigger_binding` rows — suite-owned config the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` already scopes. As written, any signed-in user could enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for bindings on suites they can't see. Now applies the same `suite_service.accessible_suite_ids` filter, with `include_all` for a workspace admin (ADR 0027), threaded through `orchestration_service.list_env_near_misses` so the API layer still reaches orchestration reads through that module.

**2. Multiple concurrent near-misses (fixed).** `.find()` → `.filter()`, one badge per mismatch naming the wrong env (`env mismatch: QA`). Also made the service sort **total** (identity fields break the `updated_at` tie) — two mismatches recorded in one ingest batch share a `func.now()` timestamp to the microsecond, so an arbitrary tie-break would reshuffle badges between refreshes.

**3. Stale badge after disabling (fixed).** `onChanged` now invalidates both reads.

**4. Test-coverage gap (fixed).** `TestNearMissWriteReadRoundTrip` drives the real `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` with a real `Connection` + `RunUpdate` and asserts the read side decodes it, plus a disabled-binding case.

**5. (judgment)** Took the cheap half — added `?suite_id=` so the panel stops pulling the whole accessible workspace per suite switch. Filed the architectural half as **#1247**.

### Second `/code-review` round found three more, all fixed
- A failed near-miss fetch rendered identically to "no mismatch" — an outage reading as healthy on the very screen built to surface it. The comment claimed it mirrored `AssetHealthLead`, but that component *does* say "unavailable". Now it says so too.
- The tooltip asserted present tense for anything inside the 48h window while `updated_at` was fetched, typed, threaded through and never rendered — a binding fixed an hour ago kept being told it was still broken. Now dated and past-tense.
- `TRIGGER_ENV_NEAR_MISS_RECENT_HOURS` missing from `.env.app.example`; added with the sibling `0 disables` convention plus `ge=0` so a negative (which would widen the window to everything) is a boot failure.

### Two things worth flagging
- **`test_assert_hygiene` (#787) caught four of my own `assert client.get(...)` calls** — `python -O` would have deleted request and assertion together. Hoisted.
- **CI caught a defect three green local runs did not.** Splitting the resilience assertions into two `it`s failed the frontend job with `TypeError: ...reading 'then'` *after* all 92 files reported green. That file's docstring had documented the exact hazard; I added a second test anyway. Folded back into one, verified over three full runs checking the **exit code** — my original local check read the "N passed" line and missed a non-zero exit entirely.

All new regression tests were mutation-checked (five mutations, each failing exactly its own test).

### Follow-ups filed
- **#1247** — read side hash-probes rather than reading stored data; the two derivations are coupled by prose + one round-trip test, not shared code. Also carries the remaining efficiency note.
- **#1248** — **pre-existing, not from this PR**: four of #1193's batch-preview tests fail under `SECRET_STORE=openbao` (the local-stack default since #1159). Reproduced on a clean `origin/main` worktree, so out of scope here — but it cost me a false-alarm triage round, and will cost every contributor one.

### Sweep status
`gh pr list --state open` → **zero open PRs**. Also merged **#1249** (progress.md re-count: 29 in `v1.1 Backlog`, 46 repo-wide, counted with `gh issue list` after the merge rather than predicted). Nothing unexpected left over.

A prior `/code-review` pass found several findings across multiple rounds. Use your judgment on fix-vs-file per CLAUDE.md's fixed-or-filed rule, but the FIRST one below is the most important and should be fixed, not filed:

1. **Access-control widening (fix this, it's a real new exposure):** `GET /orchestration/near-misses` is auth-only/workspace-wide unscoped — but `TriggerBinding` rows are suite-owned config that the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` endpoint (`backend/app/api/v1/trigger_bindings.py`) already suite-scopes (`svc.list_bindings(db, user_id=current_user.id, ...)`, docstring "List trigger bindings on accessible suites"). This PR's new endpoint lets ANY authenticated user enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for trigger bindings on suites they have zero access to — information `GET /trigger-bindings` would 403/omit for them. The route's docstring justifies this by analogy to `/orchestration/pipelines`, but that endpoint's data (`pipeline_runs`) is genuinely workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas `TriggerBinding` rows ARE suite-owned. Fix: scope the near-miss read to only bindings on suites the calling user can access, mirroring how `list_bindings` does it (likely via the same `accessible_suite_ids`-style filter used elsewhere in this codebase, e.g. in `run_service`/`incident_service`).

2. **Multiple-concurrent-near-misses-per-binding gap (fix if reasonably contained):** The frontend badge (`TriggerRow` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) picks the FIRST matching near-miss via `.find()` when more than one could be simultaneously current for the same binding (e.g. two different orchestrator connections both reporting the same DAG id against different wrong envs — literally the #1186 root cause this whole feature exists to catch). This silently hides the second live mismatch. Also related: no `ORDER BY` on the `WorkspaceHealth` read query before the Python-side sort in `list_current_env_near_misses`, so result ordering isn't guaranteed on ties, compounding the above non-deterministically.

3. **Stale badge after disabling a binding:** disabling a binding (`onChanged` in `TriggersPanel.tsx`) only reloads the bindings list, never `nearMissState` — so a mismatch badge can persist on a binding the user just disabled, until the panel remounts. Fix if cheap (e.g. also trigger a near-miss refetch on `onChanged`).

4. **Test-coverage gap (fix by strengthening tests, don't need new prod code):** the new tests exercise the write LEAF (`record_trigger_binding_env_near_miss`) directly, not the actual production write path (`orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`) — so a future change to that function's candidate-selection logic could ship green and silently desync read vs. write with no test catching it. Add at least one test that exercises the real production write path end-to-end (trigger `_record_env_near_misses` itself, not the leaf) and asserts the read side picks it up correctly.

5. **Lower priority, your judgment (fix if cheap, else file or skip):** the hash-guessing read pattern (`list_current_env_near_misses` re-derives candidate tuples and hash-probes, rather than storing/reading decodable data) is architecturally coupled to `orchestration_service`'s write-side derivation logic by a prose comment only, not shared code — a real but not urgent debt given `WorkspaceHealth.key` is an opaque hash by design (64-char PK cap). Also: the near-miss fetch on `TriggersPanel` mount refetches workspace-wide data on every suite switch (no caching), and runs even for suites with zero trigger bindings. These are efficiency/architecture observations, not correctness bugs — fix only if trivial, otherwise file as a follow-up issue rather than silently dropping.

The analogy was wrong: `pipeline_runs` is workspace-wide orchestrator telemetry with no suite-ownership concept, whereas a near-miss is derived *wholly* from `trigger_binding` rows — suite-owned config the sibling `GET /trigger-bindings` already scopes. As written, any signed-in user could enumerate `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, binding_env)` for bindings on suites they can't see. Now applies the same `suite_service.accessible_suite_ids` filter, with `include_all` for a workspace admin (ADR 0027), threaded through `orchestration_service.list_env_near_misses` so the API layer still reaches orchestration reads through that module.

**2. Multiple concurrent near-misses (fixed).** `.find()` → `.filter()`, one badge per mismatch naming the wrong env (`env mismatch: QA`). Also made the service sort **total** (identity fields break the `updated_at` tie) — two mismatches recorded in one ingest batch share a `func.now()` timestamp to the microsecond, so an arbitrary tie-break would reshuffle badges between refreshes.

**3. Stale badge after disabling (fixed).** `onChanged` now invalidates both reads.

**4. Test-coverage gap (fixed).** `TestNearMissWriteReadRoundTrip` drives the real `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses` with a real `Connection` + `RunUpdate` and asserts the read side decodes it, plus a disabled-binding case.

**5. (judgment)** Took the cheap half — added `?suite_id=` so the panel stops pulling the whole accessible workspace per suite switch. Filed the architectural half as **#1247**.

### Second `/code-review` round found three more, all fixed
- A failed near-miss fetch rendered identically to "no mismatch" — an outage reading as healthy on the very screen built to surface it. The comment claimed it mirrored `AssetHealthLead`, but that component *does* say "unavailable". Now it says so too.
- The tooltip asserted present tense for anything inside the 48h window while `updated_at` was fetched, typed, threaded through and never rendered — a binding fixed an hour ago kept being told it was still broken. Now dated and past-tense.
- `TRIGGER_ENV_NEAR_MISS_RECENT_HOURS` missing from `.env.app.example`; added with the sibling `0 disables` convention plus `ge=0` so a negative (which would widen the window to everything) is a boot failure.

### Two things worth flagging
- **`test_assert_hygiene` (#787) caught four of my own `assert client.get(...)` calls** — `python -O` would have deleted request and assertion together. Hoisted.
- **CI caught a defect three green local runs did not.** Splitting the resilience assertions into two `it`s failed the frontend job with `TypeError: ...reading 'then'` *after* all 92 files reported green. That file's docstring had documented the exact hazard; I added a second test anyway. Folded back into one, verified over three full runs checking the **exit code** — my original local check read the "N passed" line and missed a non-zero exit entirely.

All new regression tests were mutation-checked (five mutations, each failing exactly its own test).

### Follow-ups filed
- **#1247** — read side hash-probes rather than reading stored data; the two derivations are coupled by prose + one round-trip test, not shared code. Also carries the remaining efficiency note.
- **#1248** — **pre-existing, not from this PR**: four of #1193's batch-preview tests fail under `SECRET_STORE=openbao` (the local-stack default since #1159). Reproduced on a clean `origin/main` worktree, so out of scope here — but it cost me a false-alarm triage round, and will cost every contributor one.

### Sweep status
`gh pr list --state open` → **zero open PRs**. Also merged **#1249** (progress.md re-count: 29 in `v1.1 Backlog`, 46 repo-wide, counted with `gh issue list` after the merge rather than predicted). Nothing unexpected left over.

- **#1242** — Snowflake's `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` is privilege-filtered not access-denied, so a role with zero grants enumerates zero rows and #1104 records that as a healthy sync — needs a new state + UI decision to distinguish from a genuinely empty database.
- **#1243** — `/suites/{id}/batch-preview` (#1193) does an unbounded, uncancellable, blocking object listing on every keystroke pause with no `AbortController`, and now runs a user-supplied regex on the API process for the first time (ReDoS surface, `re` holds the GIL).
